IT’S MONDAY, JULY 13. Welcome to Morning Agriculture! I’m your host, Rachel Shin. Send story tips to rshin@politico.com and get in touch securely on Signal at rshin.80. Follow your favorite ag team at @Morning_Ag for more.

Want to receive this newsletter every weekday? Subscribe to POLITICO Pro. You’ll also receive daily policy news and other intelligence you need to act on the day’s biggest stories.
 

A message from Bayer:

At Bayer, we empower American farms with the smarter tools needed to advance regenerative agriculture. By providing accurate, real-time data maps, we give farmers necessary insights to improve soil health and protect the land for generations. When farmers are equipped to care for their soil with tools like real-data maps, stronger yields and a sustainable bottom line naturally follow. Learn more.
 
DRIVING THE DAY

SO MANY BILLS, SO LITTLE TIME: August recess is fast approaching, and with it, mounting urgency for Congress to advance a slew of ag legislation.

The Senate farm bill awaits a markup, and President Donald Trump has requested over $11 billion in farm assistance in a supplemental package with military funding.

Then there’s the perennial push for year-round nationwide E15 sales and other nagging question marks, like the effort to undo hemp sale restrictions, set to take effect in November. The weeks between now and August will be about triaging.

“I wish we could get a farm bill before the election, but I think that's going to come after the election,” Sen. Chuck Grassley (R-Iowa) told reporters last week. “E15 is very critical to farmers voting in the midterm elections, and so I would expect it to be at least in September, but there's no reason it couldn't be done in July.”

Senate Ag Chair John Boozman (R-Ark.) told your host in a statement that he is looking forward to marking up the farm bill during this work period and “ensuring the President’s supplemental includes the funding necessary to meet the needs of farmers.”

“There's real momentum to advancing policies that help farmers, and I'm committed to working with my colleagues to make that happen,” Boozman added.

Republicans are returning to intraparty disarray after House GOP leaders canceled votes on major bills before the Fourth of July recess. After a group of GOP hard-liners derailed progress at the end of June, some Republicans questioned whether the rest of the summer will be a wash.

The unexpected death of South Carolina Republican Lindsey Graham over the weekend complicates the picture in the Senate, narrowing the already-slim GOP majority. The majority must also account for the absence of Sen. Mitch McConnell (R-Ky.), who has been hospitalized for nearly a month after falling. He said Sunday that he will return to the Senate after his recovery but has not specified when.

In the lower chamber, Rep. Andy Barr (R-Ky.) is preparing to introduce a bipartisan bill on hemp regulation as soon as Tuesday that would roll back some of the language that the industry considers a ban on its products, according to two people familiar with the plan who were granted anonymity to discuss it.

A spokesperson for Barr did not respond to a request for comment.

Lawmakers supportive of the industry have scrambled to undo or delay the limitations on hemp products, which were included in the shutdown-ending funding bill passed last fall, before they go into effect this November. McConnell played a key role in pushing the restrictions through.

Then there’s House Ag Chair G.T. Thompson’s (R-Pa.) farm labor bill, which must receive Judiciary Chair Jim Jordan’s (R-Ohio) blessing to get a markup, as it must flow through his committee. Jordan told MA before the Fourth of July recess that he was undecided on whether to take up the legislation.
 

A message from Bayer:
 
AROUND THE AGENCIES

PUTTING ON THE RITZ: Rollins is slated to attend a dinner at George Washington’s Mount Vernon this evening, according to a copy of an event flyer obtained by POLITICO, Jacob writes in.

Attendees may pay from $7,500 to $15,000 to sponsor the event, according to the flyer.

For $15,000, a sponsor can get a table of 12 at the event, prominent name placement on promotional materials and “tailored branding input, including opportunities to provide digital content.”

The event will celebrate 250 years of American agriculture and its future and is co-hosted by Mount Vernon Ladies’ Association.

A digital form for sponsorship pledges linked in the event flyer states that “an ‘Ag250 Sponsor Invoice’ will follow with payment instructions to CropLife America.” CLA is a trade association representing the pesticide industry.

“CropLife America offered to be the point of coordination for the event,” CLA spokesperson Tonya Parish told MA in a statement. “The event is not designed to generate a profit, and any incidental proceeds will be donated to youth agricultural organizations and Mount Vernon.”

USDA did not respond to a request for comment about the event and CropLife’s involvement. Mount Vernon did not respond to a request for comment about the event.
 

A message from Bayer:

At Bayer, we believe in delivering smarter, practical tools directly to American farmers. Through advanced digital platforms, we provide accurate, real-time data maps with insights on moisture, nutrients, and compaction. This gives farmers the information they need to unlock their soil's full potential.

We empower growers to advance regenerative agriculture, helping to secure a financially sustainable future with boosted yields.

Learn more.
 
BIOFUELS FIGHT

MA EXCLUSIVE: A new poll out today charted record-high voter support for E15 fuel and year-round E15 sales legislation.

The poll, conducted by Morning Consult for the Renewable Fuels Association, comes after the House passed a year-round nationwide E15 bill in May. The bill is now in the Senate and has stalled as lawmakers deliberate on the best path forward for it, whether as a standalone or part of an upcoming package. The legislation, iterations of which have been introduced in many congresses, has been difficult to pass due to competing ag and small oil refineries interests.

The poll found that 75 percent of registered voters surveyed backed expanding the availability of the ethanol blend and 71 percent supported federal legislation allowing its sale year-round.

“The Senate has a clear opportunity to deliver what voters want by making E15 available year-round, nationwide,” RFA President and CEO Geoff Cooper said in a statement.

“The House has already passed year-round E15 legislation, and President Trump has repeatedly called on Congress to make this a priority,” he added.

item.title: ‘It's going to decimate the agency’
item.content:encoded:
Delivered every Monday by 10 a.m., Weekly Agriculture examines the latest news in agriculture and food politics and policy.
 

By Rachel Shin

With help from Marcia Brown and Oliver Ward

The Agriculture Department is undergoing a sweeping reorganization. | Getty Images
QUICK FIX

— Agriculture Department employees continue to warn that a massive reorganization plan will degrade the quality of their work.

— Ag representatives are set to join U.S. trade negotiators in Mexico this week as bilateral U.S.-Mexico-Canada Agreement review talks continue.

— A Democratic senator plans to introduce a pair of bills targeting consolidation in the ag economy and wage standards.

IT’S MONDAY, JULY 20. Welcome to Morning Agriculture! I’m your host, Rachel Shin. Send pitches to rshin@politico.com. Contact me securely on Signal to share tips at rshin.80. Follow us at @Morning_Ag for more.

Burns will also anchor a refreshed Playbook Podcast, and MEGAN MESSERLY will join Playbook as a contributor to the newsletter and podcast. Read more here.

DRIVING THE DAY

INTERNAL UNEASE: USDA employees say major programs, including international food aid and agriculture research, could break down due to a department reorganization that is relocating many USDA jobs across the country.

Collin Bradley, president of the AFSCME Local 3976 union that represents Foreign Agricultural Service workers, told MA the billions of dollars that flow through Food for Peace — the United States' international food aid program — are “going to be managed by less than 10 people who are staying in D.C.”

“Foreign service officers are going to be pretty screwed” as well, he said, because of the relocation of the Global Services branch that manages operations for U.S. embassies abroad.

FAS workers were told Friday that more than one-third of them have been asked to relocate, Marcia reported.

Food safety groups and experts separately asked Ag Secretary Brooke Rollins on Friday to pause the proposed department’s relocation of its Environmental Microbial and Food Safety Laboratory out of the Beltsville Agricultural Research Center.

“The loss of highly specialized scientific expertise would be substantial,” the experts wrote in a letter. “Past USDA relocations have shown that such moves often result in significant staff attrition, leading to gaps in institutional knowledge and reduced effectiveness in serving agricultural stakeholders.”

Workers in other USDA agencies similarly worried that the quality of the department’s work could be a shadow of itself once the restructuring is complete.

“It's just bad for agricultural research, and everybody is just really in a bad place mentally,” said an Agricultural Research Service employee, granted anonymity to discuss the internal mood.

USDA rejected that the reorganization would be detrimental to research.

“The Department has made clear the reorganization is a regimented, multi-step process, and that specific to research, all continues without interruption, except the research Congress chose to defund,” USDA spokesperson Michael Abboud said in a statement.

Both ag research and foreign service employees are predicting high attrition that could wipe out expertise.

FAS conducted a survey that found only 4 percent of people said they would relocate to Kansas City, Missouri — the hub where USDA is reassigning most of the agency, according to Bradley.

“It's going to decimate the agency,” Bradley told MA.

MA readers will recall: A coalition of unions and other groups renewed efforts to halt the reorganization, citing documents showing that USDA expects nearly a quarter of its employees to quit rather than relocate.

The reorganization was intended to reduce USDA's workforce “by approximately 23,177 which is a 23% overall reduction,” according to the 2025 internal planning documents.
TRADE TALKS

ON THE LAMB: U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer held a roundtable with sheep producers on trade policy in Utah Friday following his directive last week to the International Trade Commission to investigate the impact of lamb imports on the domestic industry.

Carson Jorgensen, sheep producer and former chair of the Utah Republican Party, hosted Greer at Skyline Sheep Company and accompanied him on a tour of public lands used for grazing.

“[Greer] had a very specific interest in agriculture and manufacturing,” Jorgensen told MA Sunday. “They want people to come back and bring manufacturing jobs back to the United States, and they want to protect domestic agriculture, and they were very bullish on the trade deficit.”

The ITC will determine whether imports are causing injury to American producers. If so, it will make recommendations for redress, which could include tariffs.

Lamb and mutton imports from New Zealand and Australia had secured over 70 percent of the U.S. market as of 2024, according to the American Sheep Industry Association.

Jorgensen and a group of other sheep industry advocates submitted a letter to the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative in early 2025 urging it to launch the investigation into foreign lamb imports.

Jorgensen said Greer has been “pretty vocal since the beginning that he's in favor of these tariffs.”

ROUND THREE: Representatives from multiple U.S. industries will be heading to Mexico this week with trade negotiators as bilateral talks on the USMCA review advance, Oliver writes in.

Industries including agriculture and steel will be represented among the delegation, according to four people familiar with the plans, granted anonymity because they were not cleared to brief the media on the closed-door discussions.

The details: Greer will meet with Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum and Secretary of the Economy Marcelo Ebrard during his three-day visit to Mexico City, which begins Wednesday, according to USTR. Among the topics the two sides are looking to discuss are steel and aluminum derivatives, labor and agriculture.

The Trump administration is expected to leave the statutory text of the agreement unchanged to avoid having Congress vote on changes to the deal, preferring to use interpretive agreements, annexes or side letters to make adjustments.

It has, however, shared some portions of texts under discussions with relevant industries, two of the people familiar with the plans told Morning Trade.

The text goes beyond written demands, one of them said, calling it “legalese.”

“It's actual negotiating text that would be part of the agreement that gets signed,” they added.

Meanwhile, Canada continues to take flak, with President Donald Trump issuing another tariff threat Friday, this time over the dangerous air quality in U.S. cities caused by Canadian wildfires.

“We are holding Canada responsible for the fact that they are not properly maintaining their Forests, and Brush therein,” Trump posted on Truth Social Friday, suggesting the cost of pollution will be “added to the tariffs.”
ON THE HILL

MA EXCLUSIVE: Sen. Peter Welch (D-Vt.) is set to introduce a pair of bills that aim to weaken consolidation in the ag market and set new standards for wages and working conditions for food companies that do business with the federal government.

Sens. Cory Booker (D-N.J.), Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) and Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) co-sponsored the Fairness for Small-Scale Farmers and Ranchers Act, which would enact a moratorium on future corporate mergers of big food and ag companies. The bill would also reinstate mandatory country-of-origin labeling for beef.

The Agricultural Worker Justice Act, co-sponsored by Booker, Sanders and Sens. John Fetterman (D-Pa.) and Ron Wyden (D-Ore.), would prohibit USDA from buying meat, poultry or processed food made by workers paid below the prevailing wage rate in their area. It directs the Labor Department to determine prevailing rates.

“Rapid consolidation has jeopardized the well-being and vitality of farms across America — we can’t let that happen,” Welch said in a statement. “We also need urgent, commonsense safeguards to protect workers in the agricultural industry who face hazardous and exploitative working conditions.”
PROPOSITION 12

MA EXCLUSIVE PART 1: More than 700 veterinarians sent a letter to members of Congress urging them to keep the Save Our Bacon Act out of the farm bill and other legislative vehicles.

The Save Our Bacon Act would roll back California’s Proposition 12, which sets standards for animal confinement for food products sold in the state. It was included in the House-passed version of the farm bill but left out of the Senate’s version.

“This harmful legislation would strip states and localities of their rights to pass a wide range of measures protecting animal welfare and public health,” the veterinarians wrote.

The letter was organized by Humane Veterinary Medical Alliance, the veterinary division of Humane World for Animals.

MA EXCLUSIVE PART 2: A July poll out of Iowa found that nearly twice as many voters oppose the Save Our Bacon Act as support it.

The poll of 625 registered Iowa voters took place earlier this month. It was conducted by Mason-Dixon Polling and Strategy and commissioned by the Defeat EATS coalition.

In every congressional district in Iowa except the 4th District, more voters said they oppose the law than support it, the poll found.

Democrats were more likely than Republicans to oppose the bill, and 53 percent of independents said they opposed it.
Industry Intel

UNO REVERSE: Bayer is withdrawing its request that the Trump administration impose countervailing duties on glyphosate imports from China after backlash from the agriculture industry, as our Grace Yarrow reported.

The parent company of pesticide giant Monsanto filed a petition last month with the Commerce Department’s International Trade Administration and the U.S. International Trade Commission, arguing that Chinese competitors benefit from unfair pricing that hurts U.S.-based glyphosate producers including its Ruveon subsidiary.

“Since filing our petitions, we have engaged directly with farmers and agricultural trade associations to hear their perspectives,” Ruveon said in a statement Friday announcing the retraction of the petition. “Today's decision reflects our commitment to putting farmers first and meeting their evolving needs, especially during this challenging farm economy.”

Read more from Grace here.
Row Crops

— Democrats see an opening in rural states for the first time in decades. In Iowa, it’s about water, Tom Philpott and Nina B. Elkadi report for POLITICO Magazine.

— Seafood Supply Co., a Dallas seafood wholesaler, was sentenced to pay a $250,000 fine for falsifying the country of origin for its salmon.

— Taylor Farms is recalling its Mexican-grown iceberg lettuce from the U.S. after American authorities linked the lettuce to a parasitic outbreak. (The Wall Street Journal)

— The Independent Beef Association of North Dakota sent a letter to the Commodity Futures Trading Commission in opposition to the agency’s new Beef Trim futures and options contracts, saying that the contracts “will place a fictitious value on beef trim.”
